newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's unemployment woes to continue, study says.
newsitem.headline: Canada's unemployment woes to continue, study says.

text.p: Strong economic growth during the next two years may end up aggravating rather than improving Canada's high unemployment rate, according to a study by the brokerage arm of one of Canada's leading banks.
The study, released on Wednesday by CIBC Wood Gundy, suggested the gradual return of more than 700,000 labor force drop-outs will result in a "sticky" jobless rate.
A job recovery would spark a much larger bounce back in labor force growth than that which followed the 1981-1982 recession, the study said.
Canada's current unemployment rate is 9.7 percent.
That number jumps dramatically when labor participation rates, which measure the number of Canadians either working or looking for work, are factored in.
Canada's unemployment would be 13.9 percent if not for an unprecedented three-percentage point drop in participation rates since the recession, said Jeff Rubin, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

"Forecasts that call for a rapidly falling jobless rate on the basis of the current participation rates assume that nearly 750,000 Canadians who have dropped out of the labor force will become permanently marginalized in the economy," Rubin said.
The study assumed that a base of 225,000 news jobs are needed to absorb the annual increase in the working-age population.
About 70,000 Canadians would re-enter the labor force for every 100,000 new jobs created over the base, the study concluded.

With more workers coming out of the woodwork as job creation picks up, the economy would have to create close to a million jobs during the next two years just to get unemployment down one percentage point, Rubin said.
